content: Insulin inhalation is a medication used to manage blood sugar levels in individuals with diabetes. It is prescribed for people with type 1 diabetes, where the body does not produce insulin, and for people with type 2 diabetes, where the body does not use insulin effectively. In type 1 diabetes, it is used alongside long-acting insulin. In type 2 diabetes, it can be used alone or in combination with other medications. This medication is a synthetic, short-acting form of human insulin that begins to work within 10 to 20 minutes after inhalation and remains effective for approximately 6 hours. It helps lower blood sugar by facilitating the movement of glucose from the bloodstream into body tissues for energy use and by reducing glucose production in the liver. Insulin inhalation is available as a powder that is administered through a specially designed inhaler. It is typically used immediately before meals, within 10 minutes of eating. It is essential to follow the instructions provided by your doctor or pharmacist and to use the medication exactly as prescribed. Do not alter the dose, frequency, or type of insulin without consulting your doctor. Insulin inhalation helps control diabetes but does not cure it, so it is important to continue using it even if you feel well. If you stop using it or switch to another type of insulin, you must first consult your doctor. When starting insulin inhalation, your doctor may adjust the doses of your other diabetes medications, such as long-acting insulin or oral diabetes drugs. Your dose of insulin inhalation may also need to be adjusted during treatment. The powder comes in small foil packets called blisters, which should not be opened or punctured manually. The blister is opened automatically when placed in the inhaler. Do not swallow the contents of the blister or attempt to inhale them without the inhaler. After use, dispose of the blister in a secure trash container, keeping it out of reach of children and pets. Do not reuse blisters. If you need to substitute doses, you may use two 1-mg blisters in place of one 3-mg blister, but never use three 1-mg blisters as a substitute for a 3-mg blister, as this could result in an overdose. Always check your blood sugar levels and obtain the correct blister size as soon as possible. If you develop a cold, cough, or nasal congestion during treatment, inform your doctor. You may still be able to use the medication, but your doctor might adjust your dose or recommend more frequent blood sugar monitoring. Before using insulin inhalation, inform your doctor if you are allergic to insulin or any of the ingredients in the medication. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as some drugs may interact with insulin inhalation. Examples include beta blockers, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, oral contraceptives, and certain asthma or cold medications. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. If you smoke, have recently quit smoking, or have a history of lung conditions such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), inform your doctor. Smoking can affect the safety and effectiveness of insulin inhalation. Do not smoke while using this medication. If you start smoking, stop using the medication and contact your doctor immediately. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have a history of nerve damage, kidney disease, or liver disease, or if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform your healthcare provider that you are using insulin inhalation. Discuss with your doctor how to manage your medication if you become ill, experience stress, travel across time zones, or change your exercise routine, as these factors can affect your insulin needs. Your doctor will also advise you on how often to check your blood sugar levels and whether you need to test your blood sugar before driving or operating machinery, as low blood sugar can impair your ability to perform these tasks safely. Insulin inhalation may reduce lung function, so your doctor will perform tests to assess your lung health before and during treatment. Follow all dietary and exercise recommendations provided by your doctor or dietitian. Maintain a consistent eating schedule and avoid skipping or delaying meals, as this can disrupt blood sugar control. Alcohol can lower blood sugar levels, so consult your doctor about safe alcohol consumption while using this medication. If you miss a dose, skip it and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for the missed one. Check your blood sugar levels and contact your doctor if they are too high. This medication may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), such as shakiness, sweating, dizziness, irritability, and blurred vision, and follow your doctor's instructions for managing these symptoms. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness, requiring immediate medical attention. High blood sugar (hyperglycemia) symptoms include extreme thirst, frequent urination, and blurred vision. If untreated, hyperglycemia can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition characterized by symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, fruity-smelling breath, and rapid breathing. Seek medical care immediately if you experience these symptoms. Common side effects of insulin inhalation include cough, chest pain, mild shortness of breath, sore throat, and runny nose. Severe side effects, such as rash, hives, or wheezing, require immediate medical attention. Report any unusual symptoms to your doctor. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Do not refrigerate or freeze the medication. Dispose of any expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of an overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Overdose can occur if you take too much insulin or if you eat or exercise less than usual after taking the correct dose. Symptoms of overdose include hypoglycemia, which should be managed according to your doctor's instructions. Keep all medical appointments and regularly monitor your blood sugar and HbA1c levels as directed by your doctor. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
